CRON DST DRIFT CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Will your cron job survive daylight saving?

Paste a cron expression and an IANA timezone and see every upcoming run that falls in a spring-forward gap (the local time never happens) or a fall-back overlap (the local time happens twice) — plus a second check for the quieter failure: a scheduler that only understands UTC (GitHub Actions' own schedule: cron included) silently drifting an hour twice a year against the local time you actually meant.

Nothing is uploaded. Every computation runs in this browser using the Intl timezone database your browser already ships.

1. Check a schedule for DST-skip / DST-overlap risk

StatusLocal timeUTC instant

2. Check a fixed-UTC-only scheduler for drift

For a scheduler with no timezone field — a plain crontab on a UTC host, or GitHub Actions' schedule: cron, which its own docs say always runs in UTC — a single expression cannot hold a local wall-clock time steady across a DST-observing zone. This shows what UTC time you actually need per segment of the year, and the drift between them.

From (local calendar date)UTC offset in effectUTC clock time needed

Prefer a CLI, or want this in CI before a deploy?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

node cli.mjs next "30 2 * * *" --tz America/New_York
node cli.mjs next "30 2 * * *" --tz America/New_York --count 5 --from 2027-03-13T00:00:00Z --json
node cli.mjs drift 09:00 --tz America/New_York
node cli.mjs drift 09:00 --tz America/New_York --year 2027 --json

Get cli.mjs — Node 18+, nothing to install, no network call ever. Both subcommands exit 1 when they find DST risk, so either works as a one-line CI check before a new scheduled job ships.

What's checked

CheckHow
Spring-forward skipA cron occurrence's local wall-clock time (e.g. 02:30) does not exist on that calendar date in the chosen timezone, because clocks jumped forward past it
Fall-back overlapA cron occurrence's local wall-clock time occurs twice on that calendar date, because clocks were set back through it — both real UTC instants are reported
Fixed-UTC-cron driftA target local time is converted to UTC once per DST segment of the year; more than one distinct UTC clock time means a single fixed-UTC schedule cannot hold the local time steady

Month and day-of-week accept the standard 3-letter names (JAN–DEC, SUN–SAT), case-insensitive, anywhere a number is allowed — singly, in a list, or as a range (MON-FRI). Minute, hour, and day-of-month stay numeric. Day-of-month and day-of-week follow the standard cron rule: when both are restricted (neither is *), a date matches either one, not both — the single most common cron misreading. See why this happens, and this checker's own named limits, or how this compares to just checking a DST calendar by hand.

Common questions

Why does a cron job skip or double-fire around daylight saving?

A cron expression that names a wall-clock time (like 02:30) in a timezone that observes DST is naming a local time that, twice a year, either does not exist (spring forward: clocks jump from 02:00 straight to 03:00, so 02:30 never happens that day) or happens twice (fall back: 01:00-01:59 occurs twice). Cron implementations do not agree on what to do then — some skip the run entirely, some fire once, some fire twice — so this tool reports the ambiguity rather than guessing which scheduler you run.

Why does a schedule drift an hour twice a year even without a skip or double-fire?

Many schedulers — GitHub Actions' own schedule: cron among them, by its own documentation — always interpret the expression in UTC, with no timezone field at all. A single UTC cron expression cannot hit the same local wall-clock time year-round in any zone that observes DST: it is exactly right for half the year and off by the DST offset, almost always one hour, for the other half. That is not a skip or a double-fire, just a job that quietly runs an hour early or late for months at a time.

Does this tool know what my actual cron daemon or scheduler will do?

No, and it does not claim to. Different cron implementations genuinely disagree on spring-forward and fall-back behavior. This tool computes the two facts that are true regardless of implementation — whether a named local time exists uniquely, doesn't exist, or exists twice on a given date — and leaves the scheduler-specific behavior to your own scheduler's documentation.

Is anything uploaded?

No. Everything is computed in your browser using the standard Intl timezone database your browser already ships, and nothing you type is sent anywhere. The CLI makes no network call either — it is pure Intl/Date arithmetic.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not engineering advice, and it does not replace testing your actual scheduler's real behavior around a DST transition. It reports whether a named local time exists, doesn't exist, or exists twice, and what UTC time a fixed-UTC schedule needs per DST segment — nothing more, and it does not know what your specific cron daemon or scheduler does with a skipped or ambiguous occurrence. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get cli.mjs and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. Nothing you type is ever uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (schedule_checked, drift_checked, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also worth a pass on the same repo: Cron Heartbeat tells you when a job that is scheduled correctly still never ran, Agent Instructions Drift Check and security.txt Check are the same deterministic, no-upload, zero-dependency shape applied to a different pair of things that quietly drift apart. If the zone itself is what you are reasoning about rather than the schedule, World Clock & Daylight shows local time, sunrise and sunset side by side for as many cities as you like — the same IANA database this page uses, pointed at people instead of cron.

Free and open source. If this saved you a bad on-call morning, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-checking-a-dst-calendar-by-hand.html.text:
← back to the checker

This checker vs. checking a DST calendar by hand

The usual way to sanity-check a scheduled job against daylight saving is to look up when the clocks change this year and eyeball whether the job's time is anywhere near it. That catches the one obvious case — a job at 02:30 the week 02:00 jumps to 03:00 — and stops there. A calendar has no way to walk a real cron expression forward, tell a skip apart from an overlap, or notice a failure mode that never touches a transition date at all.

What each one is for

Checking a DST calendar is free and requires no tool: look up the transition date for your timezone, compare it to the job's time by eye. It works for the single case where the schedule's time obviously coincides with the transition hour on an obviously-matching date.

This checker uses the same IANA timezone database a calendar lookup is based on, but walks your actual cron expression forward occurrence by occurrence, resolving each local time against the real transition instants rather than comparing dates by eye. It also runs a second, unrelated check a calendar cannot express at all: whether a fixed-UTC-only scheduler holds your intended local time steady across the year.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Does clocks-change week obviously overlap my job's time?Either one. A calendar lookup answers this at a glance, and so does this checker.
Does a schedule with a step, list, or day-of-month/day-of-week combination actually land on the transition date?This checker. Working that out by eye means correctly applying cron's OR rule for restricted day fields, which is the single most common cron misreading.
Is a fall-back occurrence a skip to shrug off, or does it happen twice?This checker, which reports both real UTC instants for an ambiguous occurrence — not visible from a calendar at all.
Does my GitHub Actions schedule: cron drift against the local time I meant?This checker's separate drift check. A DST calendar has nothing to say here, because nothing is skipped or doubled — the job just runs an hour early or late for months.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?Neither. A calendar lookup involves no tool at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser.

Common questions

Isn't checking a DST calendar enough to catch a spring-forward skip?

It catches the case where the cron time and the transition hour are the same, like a 02:30 job the week clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00. It does not catch a cron expression with a step or a list in the hour or minute field, or a day-of-month/day-of-week combination, because working out which of the resulting occurrences actually lands on the transition date requires walking the schedule forward, not reading a calendar.

What does a DST calendar not tell you at all?

Two things this checker reports separately. First, a fall-back occurrence is not a skip to notice and move past — the local time genuinely happens twice, at two different UTC instants, and a calendar has no way to show you both. Second, a fixed-UTC-only scheduler (GitHub Actions' schedule: cron among them) never touches a gap or an overlap at all; it just runs an hour early or late for half the year, which does not look like a DST bug from the calendar's point of view because nothing is skipped or doubled.

Why is eyeballing the cron expression against the transition date error-prone?

Because the standard cron day-matching rule is easy to misread by hand: when both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted (neither is a wildcard), a date matches if it satisfies either field, not both. A schedule that looks like it only runs on specific dates can also fire on every matching weekday, which changes whether it actually lands on a transition date at all.

Does this replace knowing when DST transitions happen?

No, and it does not try to. It uses the same IANA timezone database your browser already ships to find the transitions itself, then walks your actual cron expression forward against them and reports which specific occurrences are affected. The transition dates are an input this tool computes for you, not something you need to already know.

Is anything I paste into either the calendar-checking process or this tool uploaded?

There is nothing to upload either way — checking a calendar involves no tool at all, and this checker runs entirely in your browser using the Intl timezone database it already ships. The CLI makes no network call either.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. They are not engineering advice, and they do not replace testing your actual scheduler's real behavior around a DST transition. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying the output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

This page names no specific product. "Checking a DST calendar by hand" describes a manual habit every developer already has access to, not any company's product or service.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

Back to the checker

why-cron-jobs-break-across-dst.html.text:
← Back to Cron DST Drift Check

Why cron jobs break across daylight saving

A cron schedule that names a wall-clock time — 30 2 * * *, "run at 02:30" — is only unambiguous in a timezone that never changes its UTC offset. Most timezones people actually live in do change it, twice a year, and a cron expression has no way to say so. That gap produces two separate, genuinely different failure modes, and both are invisible from reading the expression itself.

Failure mode 1: the local time doesn't exist, or exists twice

When clocks spring forward, the clock jumps directly from 01:59:59 to 03:00:00 — 02:00 through 02:59 never happen that day in that timezone. A job scheduled for 02:30 has nothing to run at. When clocks fall back, 01:00 through 01:59 happen twice — a job scheduled for 01:30 has two real, equally valid instants that both match. Neither case is a bug in the cron expression; both are genuine facts about the calendar that most scheduling tools never surface, because most cron parsers only ever reason about which fields match, never about whether the resulting wall-clock time is real.

Failure mode 2: a fixed-UTC scheduler silently drifts

Plenty of schedulers sidestep timezone ambiguity by not having a timezone at all — they always run in UTC. GitHub Actions' own schedule: cron is exactly this, by its own documentation. That is not itself a bug; the bug is assuming a UTC-only schedule keeps hitting the same local time year-round. It does not: 09:00 America/New_York is 14:00 UTC in January (EST, UTC-5) and 13:00 UTC in July (EDT, UTC-4). A workflow scheduled at a single fixed UTC hour is exactly right for one DST segment of the year and an hour off for the other — a defect nobody notices until someone asks "why did this run an hour late" in March or November.

What this tool checks, and what it deliberately doesn't

CheckSourceOut of scope for v0
Spring-forward skip / fall-back overlapResolving a cron occurrence's local wall-clock time against the real IANA timezone database (via Intl) and checking whether it names zero, one, or two real UTC instantsWhat your specific scheduler actually does with a skipped or ambiguous occurrence — that varies by implementation and is out of this tool's reach
Fixed-UTC-cron driftConverting a target local time to UTC once per DST segment of a year and comparing the resultsTimezones with sub-hour or unusual DST offsets are computed correctly (the underlying arithmetic is general), but the report's language assumes the common one-hour case
Cron field parsingStandard 5-field cron (minute hour dom month dow), with the standard OR rule when both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted; month and day-of-week also accept the standard 3-letter names (JAN-DEC, SUN-SAT), case-insensitiveSeconds fields and non-standard extensions (@daily, L, W)

Wiring it into CI before a scheduled job ships

Check a new or changed schedule before it merges:

- name: Check the deploy cron for DST risk
  run: node ventures/cron-dst-drift-check/cli.mjs next "30 2 * * *" --tz America/New_York

- name: Check the GitHub Actions schedule for UTC drift
  run: node ventures/cron-dst-drift-check/cli.mjs drift 09:00 --tz America/New_York

Both subcommands exit non-zero when they find DST risk, so a schedule that would skip, double-fire, or drift is caught in the same review that introduces it, rather than in an incident channel six months later.

Common questions

Isn't this just what crontab.guru or a cron parser library already does?

A cron expression parser (crontab.guru, node-cron, croniter) tells you which minutes and hours a schedule matches. None of the popular ones surface whether a specific upcoming occurrence's local wall-clock time actually exists that day, or whether a fixed-UTC-only scheduler needs a different UTC time in summer than in winter to hit the same local hour — both are timezone-arithmetic questions the field-matching layer doesn't ask.

Does this accept named months and weekdays, like JAN or MON?

Yes. Month and day-of-week accept the standard 3-letter names (JAN-DEC, SUN-SAT), case-insensitive, anywhere a number is allowed — singly ("MON"), in a list ("MON,WED,FRI"), or as a range ("JAN-MAR"). They are converted to their numeric value with a lookup table before the same numeric parser runs, so every existing rule — lists, ranges, steps, the dom/dow OR rule — applies identically either way. Minute, hour, and day-of-month stay numeric, matching every real cron implementation; a full name ("January") or a typo throws, naming the exact token it did not recognize, rather than guessing.

Can this tell me what my scheduler will actually do at a DST transition?

No, and this is a named limitation rather than a hidden one. Different cron daemons, systemd timers, and language schedulers genuinely disagree on spring-forward and fall-back behavior — some skip, some fire once, some fire twice. This tool computes the timezone fact that is true regardless of implementation (does the local time exist, not exist, or exist twice) and leaves the scheduler-specific behavior to that scheduler's own documentation.

No warranty. This page and the tool it documents report whether a named local time exists, doesn't exist, or exists twice, and what UTC time a fixed-UTC schedule needs per DST segment — nothing more. It is not engineering advice and does not know what your specific scheduler does with a skipped or ambiguous occurrence. Verify against your own scheduler's real behavior before relying on it. Back to the tool.
